Weighted Jackson Inequalities for N-Term Wavelet Approximation: Where the Muckenhoupt Characteristic Enters

Nonlinear $N$-term approximation asks how accurately a function can be represented by at most $N$ elements of a fixed wavelet system, the indices and the coefficients being allowed to depend on the function. For the target space $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ the classical answer of DeVore, Jawerth and Popov identifies the rate $N^{-s/n}$ for the Besov class $B^s_\tau(L^\tau)$ on the critical line $1/\tau = s/n + 1/p$. This note concerns the other regime, in which the smoothness class and the target space share the exponent $p$ and a Muckenhoupt weight $w$ is admitted. The rate is then tied to the number of coefficients each scale carries, and the question that remains is quantitative: on which features of the weight does the constant depend, and in what power.

The wavelet system is a pair of band-limited biorthogonal Riesz bases $\{\psi_{j,k}\}$, $\{\tilde\psi_{j,k}\}$ of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, normalized as $\psi_{j,k}(x) = 2^{jn/2}\psi(2^j x - k)$, whose generators have Fourier transforms in $C_c^\infty$ supported in an annulus $\{a \le |\xi| \le b\}$. The Meyer system is the model example; in dimension $n$ its tensor products supply $L = 2^n - 1$ generators. All weighted quantities are expressed through the cube measures $w(Q_{j,k})$ of the dyadic cubes $Q_{j,k} = 2^{-j}(k + [0,1)^n)$, never through pointwise values of $w$.

Definition (Muckenhoupt Characteristic, Weighted Besov Space, Localized Class)

For $1 < p < \infty$ and cubes $Q$ with sides parallel to the axes, $$[w]_{A_p} = \sup_{Q} \Big(\frac{1}{|Q|}\int_Q w\Big)\Big(\frac{1}{|Q|}\int_Q w^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\Big)^{p-1}, \qquad \|f\|_{\dot B^s_{p,q}(w)} = \Big(\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} 2^{jsq}\, \|\Delta_j f\|_{L^p_w}^q\Big)^{1/q},$$ where $\Delta_j$ are homogeneous Littlewood-Paley operators. The localized class $\dot B^s_{p,q}(w;Q_0)$ consists of those $f \in L^p_w \cap \dot B^s_{p,q}(w)$ that are recovered in $L^p_w$ from their wavelet expansion along the dyadic tree $\{(j,k) : j \ge 0,\ Q_{j,k} \subset Q_0\}$ of the unit cube $Q_0 = [0,1)^n$.

Theorem (Jackson-Type Inequality with Explicit Weight Dependence)

Let $s > 0$, $1 < p < \infty$, $0 < q < \infty$ and $w \in A_p$. For every $f \in \dot B^s_{p,q}(w;Q_0)$ and every integer $N \ge 1$, $$E_N(f)_{L^p_w} \le C_0\, [w]_{A_p}^{2/p}\, N^{-s/n}\, \|f\|_{\dot B^s_{p,q}(w)}, \qquad C_0 = \frac{L\,(2L)^{s/n}}{1 - 2^{-s}}\, C_M\, K_U\, K_L .$$ Here $L$ is the number of generators, $C_M = \sum_{|i| \le M} 2^{is}$ records the finite-band index $M$ comparing the Littlewood-Paley annulus with the frequency annulus of the generators, and $K_U$, $K_L$ are explicit series in the decay envelopes of the synthesis and dual generators, bounded in closed form through the Riemann zeta function. The factor $C_0$ does not depend on $N$, $f$, $q$, $w$, or the Riesz bounds of the system. Since $2/p \le 2\theta(p)$ with $\theta(p) = \tfrac{1}{2}\max\{1, (p-1)^{-1}\}$, the bound also holds with $[w]_{A_p}^{2\theta(p)}$; the two powers coincide at $p = 2$, where the dependence on $[w]_{A_2}$ is linear.

The power $2/p$ is the product of two factors $[w]_{A_p}^{1/p}$, and each is traceable to one application of two elementary inequalities for $A_p$ weights on a cube $Q$: $$\int_Q |g| \le [w]_{A_p}^{1/p}\, |Q|\, w(Q)^{-1/p} \Big(\int_Q |g|^p w\Big)^{1/p}, \qquad w(Q) \le [w]_{A_p} \Big(\frac{|Q|}{|S|}\Big)^{p} w(S), \quad S \subset Q .$$ The first is Hölder's inequality applied to $|g| = |g|\,w^{1/p}\,w^{-1/p}$; the second is its specialization to $g = \mathbf{1}_S$, a quantitative form of the doubling property. No weighted maximal-function bound is invoked, and no equivalence constant inherited from a cited wavelet characterization enters $C_0$.

Lemma (Single-Scale Two-Sided Estimate)

For a single-scale sum $r = \sum_{k \in \Lambda} c_{j,k}\psi_{j,k}$ over a finite set $\Lambda$, $$K_L^{-1}\, [w]_{A_p}^{-1/p}\, \mathcal{S}_\Lambda \;\le\; \|r\|_{L^p_w} \;\le\; K_U\, [w]_{A_p}^{1/p}\, \mathcal{S}_\Lambda, \qquad \mathcal{S}_\Lambda = 2^{jn/2}\Big(\sum_{k \in \Lambda} |c_{j,k}|^p\, w(Q_{j,k})\Big)^{1/p}.$$ The upper estimate proceeds cube by cube. After dilation to $j = 0$, on $Q_{0,k_0}$ the sum is dominated by the decay envelope $\beta_m$ of $\psi$ over the rings $|k - k_0|_\infty = m$; writing $\beta_m = \sum_{i \ge m}(\beta_i - \beta_{i+1})$ and exchanging the order of summation, the doubling inequality returns $w$ on the enlarged cube $k + [-m, m+1)^n$ to $w(Q_{0,k})$ at the cost $[w]_{A_p}(2m+1)^{np}$. The lower estimate follows from a weighted bound for the analysis coefficients combined with biorthogonality.

$p$: Weight $|x - \tfrac13|^\gamma$, $\gamma$: $s$:

The cube masses $w(Q_{j,k})$ and the characteristic $[w]_{A_p}$ are computed from closed-form averages; the extremal panel evaluates the sums of the corollary for the chosen weight, and the last panel integrates the Meyer translates of the localization example numerically. Drag horizontally to change $N$ (or $m$), hover to read values, double-click to reset.

The approximant is not chosen greedily. It is the truncation in scale along the dyadic tree: with $j_0$ the largest integer for which the first $j_0 + 1$ generations fit in the budget, $L(2^{(j_0+1)n} - 1)/(2^n - 1) \le N$, one keeps every coefficient of generation $j \le j_0$ inside $Q_0$. Maximality of $j_0$ gives $2^{-(j_0+1)s} < (2L)^{s/n} N^{-s/n}$. Each discarded generation $j > j_0$ contributes at most $L\, C_M K_U K_L\, [w]_{A_p}^{2/p}\, 2^{-js}\|f\|_{\dot B^s_{p,q}(w)}$, by the upper single-scale estimate followed by the coefficient bound $S_j(f) \le L^{1/p} C_M K_L\, [w]_{A_p}^{1/p}\, 2^{-js}\|f\|_{\dot B^s_{p,q}(w)}$, and the geometric series over $j > j_0$ closes the argument with the factor $(1 - 2^{-s})^{-1}$.

Corollary (Lower Estimate via an Extremal Family)

For $N = 2^{mn}$ let $f_N^\ast = \sum_{k} a_k \psi_{m+1,k}$ run over the $2^n N$ cubes of generation $m+1$ in $Q_0$, with $a_k = 2^{-(m+1)(s + n/2)}\, w(Q_{m+1,k})^{-1/p}$. Then $$c_\flat\, [w]_{A_p}^{-2/p} \;\le\; \frac{E_N(f_N^\ast)_{L^p_w}}{N^{-s/n}\, \|f_N^\ast\|_{\dot B^s_{p,q}(w)}} \;\le\; c_\sharp\, [w]_{A_p}^{2/p},$$ with $c_\flat$, $c_\sharp$ independent of $N$ and $w$. The normalization makes every term $|a_k|^p w(Q_{m+1,k})$ equal, so that discarding any $N$ of the $2^n N$ terms leaves the coefficient-level ratio $(1 - 2^{-n})^{1/p}\, 2^{-s}$. If $s/n$ could be replaced by $s'/n$ with $s' > s$, the lower bound would force $c_\flat [w]_{A_p}^{-2/p} \le C' N^{-(s'-s)/n}$ for every $N$, which fails as $N \to \infty$. The construction is deterministic; no claim is made that the power $2/p$ is matched in order from below.

The restriction to the dyadic tree of $Q_0$ is not a technical convenience. On the whole of $\mathbb{R}^n$ a single scale of $\dot B^s_{p,q}$ admits arbitrarily many coefficients of comparable size: for $w \equiv 1$ the sums $f_N = \sum_{k=1}^{2N} \psi_{0,k}$, of generation $0$ and translated off the cube, satisfy $E_N(f_N)_{L^p} \ge c\, \|f_N\|_{\dot B^s_{p,q}}$ uniformly in $N$, so no inequality with a decaying factor $N^{-\kappa}$ can hold on $L^p \cap \dot B^s_{p,q}$. For $n = 1$, $p = q = 2$ and the orthonormal Meyer system the ratio is exactly $E_N(f_N)_{L^2} / \|f_N\|_{L^2} = 2^{-1/2}$, which the last panel of the figure recovers by quadrature. For band-limited generators, which have no compact support, localization at the level of coefficients takes the place that approximation on a cube occupies for compactly supported systems.

What an Explicit Constant Records

An inequality $E_N(f) \le C N^{-s/n}\|f\|$ with an unspecified $C$ is a statement about the rate; the displayed factor $[w]_{A_p}^{2/p}$ is a statement about the mechanism. It separates the contribution of the weight from that of the wavelet system, shows that the Riesz bounds of the system do not enter, and identifies $p = 2$ as the exponent at which the refined and the coarser powers coincide. The scope is correspondingly delimited: the estimate concerns the homogeneous scale, the same-exponent regime $\dot B^s_{p,q}(w) \to L^p_w$ rather than the critical line $1/\tau = s/n + 1/p$, and the localized class. Whether $2/p$ is the smallest admissible power of $[w]_{A_p}$ is left open.

The result refines two earlier works listed on this site: the unweighted Jackson-type inequality for wavelet bases decomposition, and the explicit direct and inverse estimates for linear biorthogonal multiresolution projections on the inhomogeneous weighted Besov scale, where the weight enters through the norm of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator on $L^p_w$ rather than through a displayed power of $[w]_{A_p}$. The complete proofs and the closed-form majorant of $C_0$ are available as a preprint: arXiv:2609.35520

Band-Limited Functions: Paley-Wiener Spaces, Shannon Sampling, and the Cost of a Compact Spectrum

A function is band-limited when its Fourier transform vanishes outside a bounded set. With $\hat f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t) e^{-2\pi i t\xi}\,dt$, frequency measured in cycles, the Paley-Wiener space $PW_b = \{f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) : \operatorname{supp}\hat f \subset [-b, b]\}$ collects the square-integrable functions of bandwidth $b$. These are the functions from which the Shannon and Meyer wavelets are built, and whose Littlewood-Paley pieces define the Besov scale. Three facts organize the theory: a compact spectrum makes $f$ rigid, it makes $f$ recoverable from discrete samples, and it bounds every derivative of $f$ by $f$ itself.

Theorem (Paley-Wiener, 1934)

A function $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ belongs to $PW_b$ if and only if it is the restriction to $\mathbb{R}$ of an entire function $F$ of exponential type at most $2\pi b$, that is, $|F(z)| \le C_\epsilon\, e^{(2\pi b + \epsilon)|z|}$ for every $\epsilon > 0$. In that case $F(z) = \int_{-b}^{b} \hat f(\xi) e^{2\pi i z\xi}\,d\xi$ and $|F(x + iy)| \le \sqrt{2b}\,\|f\|_{L^2}\, e^{2\pi b|y|}$.

The rigidity is immediate from the theorem: an entire function vanishing on an interval vanishes identically, so a nonzero band-limited function cannot have compact support, and more generally $f$ and $\hat f$ cannot both be concentrated on sets of finite measure. This is the first cost of a compact spectrum. A band-limited wavelet, the Meyer wavelet included, is spread over the whole line, and any localization it enjoys is decay rather than support.

Theorem (Whittaker-Kotelnikov-Shannon Sampling)

If $f \in PW_{1/2}$, then $$f(t) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(n)\, \operatorname{sinc}(t - n), \qquad \operatorname{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin \pi x}{\pi x},$$ with convergence in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$, and $\|f\|_{L^2}^2 = \sum_n |f(n)|^2$. The translates $\{\operatorname{sinc}(\cdot - n)\}_{n}$ form an orthonormal basis of $PW_{1/2}$. The proof is one line of Poisson summation: the periodization $\sum_k \hat f(\xi + k)$ equals $\sum_n f(n) e^{-2\pi i n\xi}$, and multiplying by $\mathbf{1}_{[-1/2, 1/2]}$ returns $\hat f$ because the translates $\hat f(\cdot + k)$, $k \ne 0$, do not meet $[-\tfrac12, \tfrac12]$.

The same computation explains aliasing. If $\hat f$ is not contained in $[-\tfrac12, \tfrac12]$, the samples only see the periodization $\sum_k \hat f(\xi + k)$, and a frequency $f_0$ is read as $f_a = |f_0 - \operatorname{round}(f_0)|$. The sampled sequence $\cos(2\pi f_0 n)$ is then indistinguishable from $\cos(2\pi f_a n)$, and the sinc series reconstructs the latter. The second panel of the figure lets $f_0$ be dragged across the Nyquist frequency $\tfrac12$ and shows the replicas entering the band.

The second cost of a compact spectrum is the slow decay of the reconstruction kernel. Since $\operatorname{sinc}$ decays only like $|t|^{-1}$ and is not integrable, the truncated series $S_K f(t) = \sum_{|n| \le K} f(n)\operatorname{sinc}(t - n)$ converges slowly, and the error is governed by the tail of the samples rather than by the smoothness of $f$. The remedy is oversampling. If $f \in PW_b$ with $b < \tfrac12$, then every kernel $g$ with $\hat g = 1$ on $[-b, b]$ and $\hat g = 0$ outside $[-(1-b), 1-b]$ also reproduces $f$ from its integer samples, because the replicas $\hat f(\cdot + k)$, $k \ne 0$, live in $|\xi| \ge 1 - b$. Choosing the transition of $\hat g$ on $[b, 1-b]$ smooth, with the same ramp as in the Meyer construction, makes $g$ decay faster than any power, and the truncation error falls accordingly. The price is a sampling rate $1$ above the Nyquist rate $2b$ by the factor $1/(2b)$, and the gain degrades as $b \to \tfrac12$ because the transition band narrows.

Theorem (Bernstein Inequality)

If $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R})$, $1 \le p \le \infty$, and $\operatorname{supp}\hat f \subset [-b, b]$, then $$\|f'\|_{L^p} \le 2\pi b\, \|f\|_{L^p}.$$ The constant is attained in $L^\infty$ by $\cos(2\pi b t)$. Combined with the direct (Jackson) estimate for approximation by entire functions of exponential type $\sigma$, $E_\sigma(f)_p \le C\sigma^{-s}|f|_{B^s_{p,\infty}}$, it yields the classical characterization of Besov spaces through approximation by band-limited functions: $f \in B^s_{p,q}$ if and only if $\big(\sum_j (2^{js} E_{2^j}(f)_p)^q\big)^{1/q} < \infty$.

Why Band-Limited Wavelets Suit Quantitative Estimates

A wavelet whose Fourier transform lives in a fixed annulus $\{a \le |\xi| \le b\}$ inherits all three facts. Every moment vanishes, so no smoothness ceiling appears in Jackson-type estimates. Each Littlewood-Paley block $\Delta_j f$ interacts with the wavelet scales $j - M, \dots, j + M$ only, where $M$ is fixed by the two annuli; this relation is exact rather than approximate, and it is what produces the finite constant $C_M$ in the weighted Jackson inequality of the approximation-theory series. The rigidity, however, forbids compact support, so any localization, for instance the restriction to the dyadic tree of a cube, must be imposed at the level of the coefficients rather than obtained from the support of the generators.

Several directions lie outside this note. Sampling on non-uniform sets is governed by Landau's density conditions and, for perturbations of the integers, by Kadec's $\tfrac14$ theorem; in several variables the Paley-Wiener-Schwartz theorem ties the growth of the extension to the support function of a convex spectrum; and at the endpoints $p = 1$ and $p = \infty$ the sinc series may fail to converge without additional decay of the samples. The three panels above remain within the classical one-dimensional setting, where every statement can be checked numerically against its closed form.

Meyer Wavelet Band-limited Wavelets Partition of Unity Decay and Smoothness September 2026 14 min read

The Meyer Wavelet: Orthonormality Built in the Frequency Domain

In 1985 Yves Meyer set out to show that no orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ of the form $\{2^{j/2}\psi(2^j t - k)\}_{j,k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ could consist of Schwartz functions, and constructed one instead. Strömberg had already produced an orthonormal wavelet basis of spline type in 1982, with finite smoothness and exponential decay, but Meyer's construction was the first with $\psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$, and it is written entirely on the Fourier side. The construction is short enough to verify line by line, and it exposes the mechanism behind every orthonormal wavelet: a partition of unity in frequency whose pieces overlap in a controlled way.

The only free ingredient is a ramp $\nu : \mathbb{R} \to [0,1]$ with $\nu(x) = 0$ for $x \le 0$, $\nu(x) = 1$ for $x \ge 1$, and the symmetry $\nu(x) + \nu(1-x) = 1$. The polynomial $\nu(x) = x^4(35 - 84x + 70x^2 - 20x^3)$ on $[0,1]$ is the standard choice and belongs to $C^3$; the cubic $x^2(3 - 2x)$ gives a $C^1$ ramp, and $\nu(x) = e^{-1/x}/(e^{-1/x} + e^{-1/(1-x)})$ gives a $C^\infty$ one. With angular frequency $\omega$ and $\hat f(\omega) = \int f(t) e^{-i\omega t}\,dt$, the scaling function and the wavelet are defined through their Fourier transforms.

Definition (Meyer Scaling Function and Wavelet)

$$\hat\phi(\omega) = \begin{cases} 1, & |\omega| \le \tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \\ \cos\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\nu(\tfrac{3|\omega|}{2\pi} - 1)\big), & \tfrac{2\pi}{3} \le |\omega| \le \tfrac{4\pi}{3}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \qquad \hat\psi(\omega) = e^{i\omega/2} \begin{cases} \sin\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\nu(\tfrac{3|\omega|}{2\pi} - 1)\big), & \tfrac{2\pi}{3} \le |\omega| \le \tfrac{4\pi}{3}, \\ \cos\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\nu(\tfrac{3|\omega|}{4\pi} - 1)\big), & \tfrac{4\pi}{3} \le |\omega| \le \tfrac{8\pi}{3}, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}$$ The factor $e^{i\omega/2}$ makes $\psi$ real and symmetric about $t = -\tfrac12$, and $\psi(t) = \tfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{2\pi/3}^{8\pi/3} |\hat\psi(\omega)| \cos\big(\omega(t + \tfrac12)\big)\,d\omega$.

Orthonormality of the integer translates of $\phi$ is equivalent to $\sum_{k} |\hat\phi(\omega + 2\pi k)|^2 = 1$. On $|\omega| \le \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ only $k = 0$ contributes and the sum is $1$. On $\tfrac{2\pi}{3} \le \omega \le \tfrac{4\pi}{3}$ exactly two terms survive, $k = 0$ and $k = -1$, and with $x = \tfrac{3\omega}{2\pi} - 1 \in [0,1]$ one has $\tfrac{3|\omega - 2\pi|}{2\pi} - 1 = 1 - x$. The symmetry of $\nu$ then gives $$|\hat\phi(\omega)|^2 + |\hat\phi(\omega - 2\pi)|^2 = \cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\nu(x)\big) + \cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}(1 - \nu(x))\big) = \cos^2\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\nu(x)\big) + \sin^2\!\big(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\nu(x)\big) = 1 .$$ The same identity, read on the annulus, yields $|\hat\phi(\omega)|^2 + |\hat\psi(\omega)|^2 = |\hat\phi(\omega/2)|^2$ and hence the dyadic partition of unity $\sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}} |\hat\psi(2^{-j}\omega)|^2 = 1$ for $\omega \ne 0$. The whole construction reduces to the single relation $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$ placed at the right frequencies.

Theorem (Meyer, 1985; Lemarié-Meyer, 1986)

For every ramp $\nu$ as above, $\{\phi(\cdot - k)\}_{k}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V_0$, the spaces $V_j = \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{2^{j/2}\phi(2^j \cdot - k)\}$ form a multiresolution analysis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, and $\{\psi_{j,k}(t) = 2^{j/2}\psi(2^j t - k)\}_{j,k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. Since $\hat\psi$ vanishes on $|\omega| < \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$, every moment of $\psi$ vanishes. If $\nu \in C^m$, then $\hat\psi \in C^m_c$ and $|\psi(t)| \le C_m (1 + |t|)^{-m}$; if $\nu \in C^\infty$, then $\psi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R})$. The two-scale symbol $m_0(\omega) = \sum_{k} \hat\phi(2\omega + 4\pi k)$ is $2\pi$-periodic and smooth but not a trigonometric polynomial, so the refinement filter $h[n]$ is infinite.

The decay of $\psi$ is dictated by the smoothness of $\hat\psi$, and that smoothness is dictated by $\nu$ at the four band edges $\pm\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$, $\pm\tfrac{8\pi}{3}$. With the cubic ramp, $\hat\psi$ is $C^1$ with a jump in its second derivative, and two integrations by parts give $|\psi(t)| \asymp |t|^{-3}$ along a sequence; the degree-seven ramp raises this to $|t|^{-5}$; the $C^\infty$ ramp gives decay faster than every power. The measured log-log slopes in the third panel are close to $-3$ and $-5$ for the polynomial ramps and steepen without bound for the $C^\infty$ ramp. Decay faster than every power is the limit: if $|\psi(t)| \le C e^{-\epsilon|t|}$, then $\hat\psi$ would extend analytically to the strip $|\operatorname{Im}\omega| < \epsilon$, which is incompatible with $\hat\psi$ vanishing on an interval unless $\psi \equiv 0$.

Meyer and Daubechies: Two Sides of One Obstruction

The Meyer and Daubechies constructions occupy opposite ends of the same trade-off. Meyer fixes a compact spectrum and obtains $C^\infty$ regularity, all vanishing moments and super-polynomial decay, but no compact support and an infinite filter. Daubechies fixes compact support and a finite filter, and pays with finite regularity and a finite number $N$ of vanishing moments. The consequence for approximation theory is direct. A Jackson-type estimate on the Besov scale $B^s_{p,q}$ with Daubechies wavelets requires $s < N$, whereas the Meyer system imposes no ceiling on $s$. In addition, because $\hat\psi$ lives in a fixed annulus, each Littlewood-Paley block of a function interacts with only a bounded number of wavelet scales. This finite-band property is the structural input behind the explicit constant $C_M$ in the weighted Jackson inequality discussed in the approximation-theory series of this blog.

Two limitations should be stated. Since the filter $h[n]$ is infinite, the fast wavelet transform must be realized through the FFT on a periodized grid rather than through finite convolutions, and truncating $h$ destroys orthonormality to the order of the truncated tail. Moreover, the time localization, although super-polynomial, depends on the constants in the derivatives of $\nu$: the $C^\infty$ ramp above is asymptotically the fastest, yet on moderate windows the degree-seven ramp decays faster, and the third panel shows the $C^\infty$ envelope overtaking it only for $|t|$ of the order of $50$. The tensor-product extension to $\mathbb{R}^n$ supplies $2^n - 1$ band-limited generators with the same properties, and it is the system used as the model case of band-limited biorthogonal bases in weighted estimates.

Effective Dimension Functional ANOVA Ridge Functions Active Subspace September 2026 13 min read

Effective Dimension: Where the Ambient Dimension Goes When the Rate Improves

The entropy lower bound of the previous note is a statement about a ball in a smoothness space, and the only way past it is to work in a smaller class. Effective dimension is the name given to several distinct ways of specifying such a class, all sharing one feature: the exponent in the convergence rate is governed by a quantity $d_0$ that can be much smaller than the ambient dimension $d$, while $d$ itself does not vanish but withdraws into a prefactor. Making that prefactor explicit is what separates a usable statement from a slogan, because it is the prefactor that determines at which budget the improved exponent begins to pay.

The organizing device is the functional ANOVA decomposition. For $f \in L^2$ on a product domain with a product measure, there is a unique expansion into mutually orthogonal terms indexed by coordinate subsets, $$f(x) = \sum_{T \subseteq \{1,\dots,d\}} f_T(x_T), \qquad \int f_T(x_T)\, d\mu_i(x_i) = 0 \ \ \text{for all } i \in T,$$ and orthogonality gives the exact variance decomposition $\sigma^2(f) = \sum_{T \neq \emptyset} \sigma^2(f_T)$. The order $|T|$ counts how many coordinates genuinely interact in a term. Two notions of effective dimension are then standard: the truncation dimension is the smallest $d_0$ such that the terms with $T \subseteq \{1,\dots,d_0\}$ carry a prescribed fraction of the variance; the superposition dimension is the smallest $d_0$ such that the terms with $|T| \le d_0$ do. It is the superposition notion that controls approximation rates, because it bounds the order of interaction rather than the identity of the active coordinates.

Theorem (Rate on Coordinate-Subset Additive Classes)

Let $\Omega = \prod_{i=1}^{d}\Omega_i$ be a bounded product domain and let $$\mathcal{S}^s_{d_0}(\Omega) = \Big\{ f = \sum_{|T| = d_0} g_T(x_T) \ : \ g_T \in B^s_{p,q}(\Omega_T) \Big\}$$ be the class of functions carrying interactions of order exactly $d_0$. For localized shallow networks of width $N$ the approximation error satisfies $$E^\flat_N(f)_{L_p(\Omega)} \le C'' N^{-s/d_0} \,|f|_{\mathcal{S}^s_{d_0}(\Omega)}, \qquad C'' = \Lambda\, C_1\, (2\kappa)^{s/d_0} \binom{d}{d_0}^{s/d_0},$$ where $\kappa = (\nu' + d\nu'')/(\nu' + d_0\nu'')$ is the localized coordinate embedding factor and $\Lambda$ is the geometric fiber measure bound. The decay exponent depends on $d_0$ alone; the ambient dimension enters only through $C''$.

The prefactor is not a technicality. Since $\binom{d}{d_0}$ is the number of coordinate faces of order $d_0$, the width budget must be shared among them, and the resulting factor $\binom{d}{d_0}^{s/d_0}$ can be very large: for $d = 20$ and $d_0 = 2$ it equals $190^{s/2}$, which at $s = 2$ is $190$. Comparing the two bounds $C'' N^{-s/d_0}$ and $C N^{-s/d}$ and solving for equality identifies a crossover budget $$N^\ast \;=\; \Big(\tfrac{C''}{C}\Big)^{\frac{1}{s(1/d_0 - 1/d)}},$$ below which the ambient-dimension bound is the smaller of the two. The improvement is therefore asymptotic: it is genuine, it is eventually decisive, and it is invisible until the budget crosses $N^\ast$. A statement of this kind is only actionable when $C''$ is written down, which is why tracking it explicitly matters more than the exponent alone.

Ambient $d$: Effective $d_0$: Smoothness $s$: Interaction decay:
Interactive figure — the ANOVA panel distributes variance across interaction orders with a geometric decay and reports the superposition dimension at the $99\%$ level; the rate panel solves $C'' N^{-s/d_0} = C N^{-s/d}$ for the crossover $N^\ast$ and marks it. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, click a bar or a curve to read its value. Setting a slow interaction decay pushes the superposition dimension up and the crossover budget out, which is the quantitative form of the statement that effective dimension is a property of the function, not of the problem.

A second and inequivalent route to a small effective dimension is linear rather than combinatorial. A ridge function $f(x) = g(a^\top x)$ is constant along the $(d-1)$-dimensional hyperplanes orthogonal to $a$, so the intrinsic problem is univariate regardless of $d$; more generally $f(x) = g(A^\top x)$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ has an active subspace of dimension $k$. The two notions do not contain one another. A ridge function with a direction $a$ having all coordinates non-zero has superposition dimension $d$, since every coordinate interacts; conversely an additive function $\sum_i g_i(x_i)$ has superposition dimension $1$ but no non-trivial active subspace unless the $g_i$ are linear. Which notion is appropriate is a modelling decision, and the two lead to different algorithms: basis selection over coordinate faces in one case, and estimation of $A$ from gradient covariance in the other.

What an Effective-Dimension Claim Commits To

Effective dimension is a property of the target function, not of the estimator, so an empirical procedure cannot confer it. What a procedure can do is exploit it when present and degrade gracefully when it is not. Two consequences follow for how such claims should be read. First, the guarantee is conditional on membership in the restricted class, and unlike a smoothness assumption that condition is often checkable: the ANOVA variance shares can be estimated, and a superposition dimension of one or two is a testable hypothesis rather than an article of faith. Second, the improvement is a statement about the exponent, and the prefactor decides when it materializes; a bound that suppresses $\binom{d}{d_0}^{s/d_0}$ reports the asymptotics while withholding the information a practitioner needs. In my work on additive Besov classes the prefactor is carried in closed form for exactly this reason, and the accompanying diagnostics on the UCI educational data indicate a superposition dimension of $d_0 = 1$, which is what makes the reported rate applicable to that dataset rather than merely available in principle.

Curse of Dimensionality Covering Numbers Concentration of Measure Nonlinear Widths September 2026 14 min read

The Curse of Dimensionality Is a Theorem, Not a Difficulty: Four Ways the Exponent $d$ Appears

The phrase is Bellman's, and in the approximation-theoretic literature it names something more specific than the informal complaint that high-dimensional problems are hard. It names a family of lower bounds. On the standard smoothness classes, no method of a given budget can do better than a rate whose exponent carries $d$ in the denominator, and this is a theorem about the class rather than a shortcoming of any particular algorithm. Any claim to have escaped it must therefore be a claim to have left the class. This note collects four places where the exponent appears, each with its own mechanism, and then states the only two exits that are actually available.

The first mechanism is metric. The quantitative content is that the Sobolev or Besov unit ball is large in the sense of covering numbers, and every approximation scheme is bounded below by that size.

Theorem (Entropy Numbers of the Smoothness Ball)

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain and let $U$ be the unit ball of $B^s_{p,q}(\Omega)$, regarded as a subset of $L_p(\Omega)$. Then the covering numbers satisfy $$\log N(U, \varepsilon, L_p) \asymp \varepsilon^{-d/s}, \qquad \varepsilon \to 0^+ ,$$ equivalently the entropy numbers obey $e_n(U) \asymp n^{-s/d}$. Consequently, for any family of approximants parameterized by $n$ real numbers and depending continuously on them, the worst-case error over $U$ is bounded below by $c\, n^{-s/d}$. The exponent is not attached to a method; it is the metric entropy of the class, and it is attained by linear schemes, so nonlinearity alone buys nothing here.

The second mechanism is geometric and concerns how much of a cube is near its boundary. A grid of side $\varepsilon$ in $[0,1]^d$ has $\varepsilon^{-d}$ cells, so resolving a function to accuracy $\varepsilon$ by local averaging requires that many samples: to halve $\varepsilon$ in dimension $20$ costs a factor $2^{20}$. The same computation read in reverse says that the volume fraction of $[0,1]^d$ lying within $\delta$ of the boundary is $1 - (1-2\delta)^d$, which tends to one for any fixed $\delta$ as $d$ grows. In dimension $50$ with $\delta = 0.01$, some $63\%$ of the cube is within one hundredth of a face. Interior asymptotics are therefore not what one is measuring in high dimension.

The third mechanism concerns the unit ball itself, and it is the one most often found counterintuitive. The volume of the Euclidean unit ball, $$V_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac{d}{2} + 1\right)},$$ increases to a maximum at $d = 5$, where $V_5 \approx 5.264$, and then decreases to zero: $V_{20} \approx 0.0258$ and $V_{50} \approx 1.73 \times 10^{-13}$. The ratio of the ball's volume to that of its circumscribing cube, $V_d/2^d$, falls off super-exponentially. A uniform sample of the cube therefore almost never lands in the inscribed ball once $d$ is moderate, which is why rejection sampling and any scheme resting on volumetric coverage degrade so abruptly.

The fourth mechanism is probabilistic. For $X, Y$ independent and uniform on $[0,1]^d$, the squared distance $\|X - Y\|^2$ is a sum of $d$ independent contributions, each with mean $1/6$ and finite variance. The law of large numbers gives $\|X - Y\| \approx \sqrt{d/6}$ with fluctuations of order $1$, so the relative spread of pairwise distances is $O(d^{-1/2})$ and tends to zero. In the limit, all points are approximately equidistant: the ratio of the farthest to the nearest neighbour distance approaches one. Nearest-neighbour rules, kernel methods with a fixed bandwidth, and any procedure that reads a distance as a similarity lose their discriminating power for this reason, and the loss is a property of the ambient geometry rather than of the data.

Dimension $d$: Smoothness $s$:
Interactive figure — the volume panel evaluates $V_d = \pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(d/2+1)$ through a Lanczos approximation to the Gamma function, and the distance panel draws an actual Monte-Carlo sample of $\|X-Y\|$ for uniform points in $[0,1]^d$, recomputed when $d$ changes. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, click a curve or a bar to read its value. Raising $d$ flattens the rate curve, empties the unit ball, and collapses the distance histogram onto a single spike.

Given that the lower bound is a theorem, the only honest responses are to change the class or to change what is being measured. Two changes are known to work, and they are the two that recur throughout the literature.

The Two Available Exits

The first is to impose structure on the interaction pattern. If $f$ depends on its coordinates only through subsets of size $d_0 \ll d$, as in the coordinate-subset additive classes $\mathcal{S}^s_{d_0}(\Omega)$, or only through a low-dimensional linear image as in a ridge function $f(x) = g(A^\top x)$, then the effective quantity replacing $d$ in the exponent is $d_0$ or the rank of $A$. The ambient dimension does not disappear: it re-enters through a prefactor, typically of the order $\binom{d}{d_0}^{s/d_0}$, so the improvement is asymptotic in $N$ rather than uniform. The second is to change the norm in which the error is measured, or to accept a randomized guarantee. Barron's class is the canonical instance: functions whose Fourier transform has finite first moment admit $L^2$ approximation by sums of $n$ ridge functions at rate $n^{-1/2}$ with a constant independent of $d$. The rate is dimension-free, but the class is defined by a condition whose verification is itself dimension-sensitive, and the improvement is stated for the $L^2$ norm rather than uniformly. Neither exit repeals the entropy lower bound. Each identifies a proper subclass on which the bound does not apply, which is the only thing that can be done.

How to Read a Dimension-Free Claim

When a rate is advertised as free of the ambient dimension, three questions settle what has actually been shown. Which class is the estimate uniform over, and is membership in that class checkable? Where did $d$ go — into a prefactor, into a norm on the right-hand side, or into a probabilistic qualifier? And is the guarantee a genuine approximation bound, or a bound on a surrogate such as the empirical risk? A claim that survives all three is a claim about a subclass, stated honestly. In my own work on shallow networks over additive Besov classes the answers are recorded explicitly: the rate is $N^{-s/d_0}$ governed by the effective dimension, the ambient dimension is confined to the tracked prefactor $\Lambda C_1 (2\kappa)^{s/d_0}\binom{d}{d_0}^{s/d_0}$, and the estimate is non-asymptotic in the $L_p$ norm. Making the prefactor visible is what allows a reader to determine at which budget $N$ the improved exponent actually takes effect.

Bedrosian Identity Hilbert Transform Analytic Signal Fourier Multipliers September 2026 13 min read

When Does the Hilbert Transform Factor Through a Product? The Bedrosian Identity and Its Failure

The Hilbert transform is linear but not multiplicative: in general $\mathscr{H}(fg) \neq f\,\mathscr{H}g$, and there is no reason to expect otherwise from a singular integral operator. What Bedrosian observed in 1963 is that a purely spectral hypothesis restores the factorization exactly, and the hypothesis is checkable. This note states the identity, proves it from the multiplier representation, and then examines what happens on the other side of the hypothesis — because in applications the condition is nearly always violated to some degree, and what matters is the size of the residual rather than its vanishing.

Recall the operator. For $x \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ the Hilbert transform is the principal-value convolution $$\mathscr{H}x(t) = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x(\tau)}{t - \tau}\,d\tau ,$$ equivalently the Fourier multiplier $\widehat{\mathscr{H}x}(\omega) = -i\,\mathrm{sgn}(\omega)\,\hat{x}(\omega)$. Since $|-i\,\mathrm{sgn}(\omega)| = 1$ for $\omega \neq 0$, Plancherel gives $\|\mathscr{H}x\|_{L^2} = \|x\|_{L^2}$: the operator is a linear isometry on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, and it satisfies $\mathscr{H}^2 = -I$ on the orthogonal complement of the constants.

Theorem (Bedrosian, 1963)

Let $f, g \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $fg \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$, and suppose their Fourier transforms have separated supports: there is a bandwidth $B > 0$ with $$\operatorname{supp}\hat{f} \subseteq [-B, B], \qquad \operatorname{supp}\hat{g} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\setminus[-B, B].$$ Then $\mathscr{H}(fg) = f\cdot\mathscr{H}g$.

The proof is a statement about where the signum function is constant. We compare the two sides on the Fourier side and track the region of integration in the convolution.

Proof

The product corresponds to convolution, $\widehat{fg} = \hat{f} * \hat{g}$, so applying the multiplier gives $$\mathscr{F}\{\mathscr{H}(fg)\}(\omega) = -i\,\mathrm{sgn}(\omega)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(\omega - \xi)\,\hat{g}(\xi)\,d\xi ,$$ while the right-hand side reads $$\mathscr{F}\{f\cdot\mathscr{H}g\}(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \hat{f}(\omega - \xi)\,\big[-i\,\mathrm{sgn}(\xi)\,\hat{g}(\xi)\big]\,d\xi .$$ The two agree precisely when $\mathrm{sgn}(\omega) = \mathrm{sgn}(\xi)$ at every point where the integrand is non-zero. The integrand is supported where $\omega - \xi \in \operatorname{supp}\hat{f}$ and $\xi \in \operatorname{supp}\hat{g}$, that is where $|\omega - \xi| \le B$ and $|\xi| > B$. Write $\eta = \omega - \xi$, so $\omega = \eta + \xi$ with $|\eta| \le B$. If $\xi > B$ then $\omega = \xi + \eta > B - B = 0$, hence $\mathrm{sgn}(\omega) = 1 = \mathrm{sgn}(\xi)$. If $\xi < -B$ then $\omega = \xi + \eta < -B + B = 0$, hence $\mathrm{sgn}(\omega) = -1 = \mathrm{sgn}(\xi)$. In both cases the signum factor is constant across the support of the integrand and may be moved inside, which is the assertion. The separation is used exactly once, and it is used to prevent $\omega$ from changing sign relative to $\xi$.

The argument also shows what the hypothesis is buying, so the failure mode can be computed rather than merely feared. Take the elementary pair $f(t) = 1 + a\cos(Bt)$ and $g(t) = \cos(\omega_0 t)$. Then $\mathscr{H}[\cos(ct)] = \mathrm{sgn}(c)\sin(ct)$, and expanding the product into its three spectral lines at $\omega_0$ and $\omega_0 \pm B$ gives $$\mathscr{H}(fg) - f\,\mathscr{H}g = \tfrac{a}{2}\big[\mathrm{sgn}(\omega_0 - B) - 1\big]\sin\!\big((\omega_0 - B)t\big),$$ which vanishes identically when $\omega_0 > B$ and equals $a\sin\!\big((B - \omega_0)t\big)$ when $\omega_0 < B$. The residual therefore does not decay gradually as the supports approach: it is zero up to the crossing $\omega_0 = B$ and jumps to amplitude $a$ immediately past it, oscillating at the difference frequency $B - \omega_0$. This discontinuity in the residual as a function of the separation is the reason the Bedrosian condition is stated as a support hypothesis rather than as a smallness assumption.

Carrier $\omega_0$: Envelope bandwidth $B$: Depth $a$:
Interactive figure — every curve is evaluated from the closed forms above, not sampled numerically, so the residual shown is the exact quantity $\tfrac{a}{2}[\mathrm{sgn}(\omega_0-B)-1]\sin((\omega_0-B)t)$. Drag to pan the time axis, scroll to zoom, click a spectral line to read its position. Moving the carrier below the envelope bandwidth crosses $\omega_0 = B$: the two sides of the identity separate at once, and the envelope panel shows $|z|$ departing from $|f|$ in the same instant.

The identity is what makes the analytic signal interpretable. Given a real $x$, the analytic signal is $z = x + i\mathscr{H}x = A e^{i\varphi}$, and one calls $A = |z|$ the instantaneous amplitude and $\varphi' $ the instantaneous frequency. These names are only justified when $x$ actually admits a representation $x = a\cos\varphi$ in which the amplitude varies slowly relative to the phase. Under the Bedrosian hypothesis with $f = a$ and $g = \cos\varphi$, the identity gives $\mathscr{H}\{a\cos\varphi\} = a\,\mathscr{H}\{\cos\varphi\} = a\sin\varphi$, whence $z = a e^{i\varphi}$ and $A = |a|$ exactly. Without the hypothesis, $A$ is still defined, but it is no longer the amplitude of anything: it mixes the two factors, and the extracted instantaneous frequency can leave the convex hull of the frequencies actually present.

The Practical Reading, and a Caution

The empirical mode decomposition of the Hilbert-Huang transform is designed to produce components on which the amplitude varies slowly relative to the phase, that is, components for which the Bedrosian hypothesis is approximately in force. The sifting procedure that produces them is algorithmic rather than analytic, so the degree of approximation is not quantified, and mode mixing can leave a component whose spectrum straddles the crossing. A transparent alternative is to place the components where the separation can be verified: assigning the slowly varying factor to a scaling space $V_J$ and the oscillatory factor to detail spaces $W_j$ makes the support condition a statement about the filter bank, checkable before the Hilbert transform is applied. The residual $\|r_{\text{Bedrosian}}\|_{L^2}$ then enters an error bound as a named term rather than remaining an unexamined modelling assumption. This is the structure adopted in the WHiAR-Net framework, where that residual is one of exactly three contributions to the total prediction error.

Two refinements deserve mention. Nuttall and Bedrosian later gave a bound on the error in the analytic-signal representation when the spectra are not disjoint, expressed in terms of the energy of $\hat{x}$ on the negative frequency axis; this converts the qualitative hypothesis into a quantitative one. Separately, Xu and Yan characterized the pairs $(f,g)$ for which the identity holds, showing that disjointness of supports in the above sense is sufficient but not necessary, and describing the exact condition in terms of the supports of $\hat{f}$ and $\hat{g}$ relative to one another. The picture that emerges is that the identity is governed by a combinatorial condition on spectral supports rather than by any smallness of a norm.

Daubechies Wavelets Refinement Equation Vanishing Moments Compact Support September 2026 16 min read

Compactly Supported Orthonormal Wavelets: What Daubechies Resolved, and What It Costs

Before 1988 the orthonormal wavelet bases available to analysts each conceded one property. The Haar system is compactly supported and orthonormal but discontinuous, so it reproduces no polynomial beyond constants and its approximation order stops at one. The Shannon system is band-limited with unlimited vanishing moments, but $\psi$ decays only like $|t|^{-1}$, so time-localization is lost. The Meyer system is $C^\infty$ and orthonormal, yet by the Paley-Wiener theorem a function with compactly supported Fourier transform cannot itself have compact support. The question left open was whether orthonormality, compact support and a prescribed number of vanishing moments can be held simultaneously. Daubechies answered it constructively, and the construction also delimits what the answer costs.

The setting is a multiresolution analysis: a nested ladder $\{V_j\}_{j \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of closed subspaces of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $V_{j+1} \subset V_j$, dense union, trivial intersection, and a scaling function $\phi \in V_0$ whose integer translates form an orthonormal basis of $V_0$. Because $\phi \in V_0 \subset V_{-1}$ and $\{\sqrt{2}\,\phi(2t-n)\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V_{-1}$, the scaling function satisfies a two-scale relation, and everything else is determined by its coefficient sequence.

Definition (Refinement Equation and Its Symbol)

The scaling function satisfies $$\phi(t) = \sqrt{2} \sum_{n} h[n]\, \phi(2t - n), \qquad h[n] = \langle \phi, \sqrt{2}\,\phi(2\cdot - n) \rangle .$$ Writing $m_0(\omega) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sum_n h[n] e^{-in\omega}$ for the symbol, the relation reads $\hat{\phi}(2\omega) = m_0(\omega)\hat{\phi}(\omega)$, and iterating gives the infinite product $\hat{\phi}(\omega) = \prod_{k=1}^{\infty} m_0(2^{-k}\omega)$. Orthonormality of the translates is equivalent to the quadrature condition $|m_0(\omega)|^2 + |m_0(\omega + \pi)|^2 = 1$, and $m_0(0) = 1$ normalizes the product. The wavelet is then $\psi(t) = \sqrt{2}\sum_n g[n]\phi(2t-n)$ with $g[n] = (-1)^n h[1-n]$.

Two structural requirements are now in tension. Compact support of $\phi$ forces $h$ to be a finite sequence, so $m_0$ is a trigonometric polynomial. Vanishing moments force that polynomial to be divisible by a high power of $(1 + e^{-i\omega})$: the condition $\int t^k \psi(t)\,dt = 0$ for $k = 0,\dots,N-1$ is equivalent to $m_0$ having a zero of order $N$ at $\omega = \pi$. The construction consists of meeting both at once.

Theorem (Daubechies, 1988)

For every integer $N \ge 1$ there exists a scaling function $\phi_N$ with $\operatorname{supp}\phi_N = [0, 2N-1]$ such that $\{\psi_{N,j,k}(t) = 2^{-j/2}\psi_N(2^{-j}t - k)\}_{j,k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and $\psi_N$ has $N$ vanishing moments. The symbol admits the factorization $$|m_0(\omega)|^2 = \cos^{2N}\!\left(\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right) P\!\left(\sin^2\tfrac{\omega}{2}\right), \qquad P(y) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \binom{N-1+k}{k} y^k ,$$ where $P$ is the minimal-degree solution of the Bezout equation $(1-y)^N P(y) + y^N P(1-y) = 1$. The passage from $|m_0|^2$ to $m_0$ is a spectral factorization supplied by the Riesz lemma, which is where the choice of which roots to retain enters and why the resulting filters are not symmetric for $N \ge 2$.

The support length is not an artifact of the construction. It is forced.

Theorem (Support-Moment Trade-off)

If $\psi$ generates an orthonormal wavelet basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and has $N$ vanishing moments, then $\operatorname{supp}\psi$ has length at least $2N-1$. The Daubechies family attains this length, so within the class of orthonormal wavelets with $N$ vanishing moments no shorter support is available. The consequence for signal analysis is direct: each additional order of polynomial suppression is paid for by two additional taps, and therefore by a wider region in which a singularity contaminates the coefficients. At scale $j$ the number of coefficients whose support meets a given singularity is proportional to $2N-1$, independently of $j$.

Vanishing moments $N$: Cascade iterations $k$:
Interactive figure — the filter taps are the actual Daubechies coefficients and the scaling function is produced by running the cascade iteration $\phi^{(k+1)}(t) = \sqrt{2}\sum_n h[n]\phi^{(k)}(2t-n)$ live, starting from the indicator of $[0,1)$. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, click a tap or a curve to read its value. Raising $N$ widens the support to $2N-1$ while the limit function becomes smoother; setting $N=1$ returns the Haar system, where the cascade is stationary after one step.

What is gained in exchange for the wider support is regularity, and the gain is slow. The Hölder exponent of $\phi_N$ grows asymptotically like $\mu N$ with $\mu \approx 0.2$, so doubling the smoothness costs roughly five additional vanishing moments and ten additional taps. Concretely, $\phi_1$ is discontinuous, $\phi_2$ is Hölder of exponent about $0.550$, $\phi_3$ about $1.088$, and $\phi_4$ about $1.618$. The sequence is increasing but never reaches $C^\infty$ at finite $N$, which is the quantitative form of the obstruction the Meyer construction meets from the other side.

Why This Matters for Approximation Rates

Vanishing moments are the mechanism behind every Jackson-type wavelet estimate. If $f \in C^\alpha$ with $\alpha \le N$, then on the support $I_{j,k}$ of $\psi_{j,k}$ one may subtract the Taylor polynomial of degree $\lfloor \alpha \rfloor$ without changing the coefficient, because $\psi_{j,k}$ annihilates it. The Hölder remainder then gives $|\langle f, \psi_{j,k}\rangle| \le C 2^{-j(\alpha + 1/2)}$, and summing the $\asymp 2^j$ coefficients at scale $j$ and the geometric series over $j \ge J$ produces $\|f - P_{V_J}f\|_{L^2} \le C 2^{-J\alpha}$. This is precisely the estimate that bounds the trend channel in the WHiAR-Net architecture, and the condition $\alpha \le N$ appearing there is exactly the requirement that the basis carry enough vanishing moments to see the regularity one is claiming. Choosing $N$ too small caps the attainable rate regardless of how smooth the signal is; choosing it too large widens the support and admits more boundary contamination. The selection is therefore a structural decision rather than a tuning parameter.

Two extensions are worth recording. Relaxing orthogonality to biorthogonality buys symmetry, which is why the Cohen-Daubechies-Feauveau family is used where linear phase matters; the cost is that analysis and synthesis bases differ, and the Riesz constants of the pair enter every estimate. Relaxing minimal support instead buys near-symmetry within the orthogonal class, giving the symlets. The exponent $\mu \approx 0.2$ governing the regularity growth is itself obtained from a joint-spectral-radius computation on the transition operators associated with $h$, which is the analytic content of the Daubechies-Lagarias analysis of the cascade.

Wavelet-Hilbert Analysis Bedrosian Identity Interpretable Machine Learning Time Series Forecasting August 2026 15 min read

WHiAR-Net: Structural Embedding of Operator Error Bounds in a Multi-Scale Forecasting Architecture

Forecasting non-stationary time series is ordinarily approached by increasing model capacity. Transformer-based architectures approximate global dependencies through attention, and they attain competitive empirical accuracy, but the mapping they realize carries no functional-analytic reading: the intermediate representations are not constrained to any identifiable manifold, and no error decomposition attaches to them. In work published in Scientific Reports (2026, 16, 23751), I propose the opposite arrangement. Rather than treating the wavelet transform as a static preprocessing step feeding a learnable black box, WHiAR-Net embeds multiresolution analysis and Hilbert spectral analysis inside the architecture, so that every component of the prediction error is bounded by a quantity available in closed form. The design is a study in mathematical parsimony rather than massive parameterization: the transform is fixed, the operator norms are tracked, and only a task-specific fusion node is learned.

The signal is segregated into two deterministically bounded channels. A regularity-dominated trend is carried by the scaling coefficients $a_J \in V_J$ and predicted by an autoregressive model on those coefficients; a transient volatility component is carried by the detail coefficients $d_j \in W_j$ and processed through the Hilbert transform. The first channel is governed by a classical Jackson-type estimate on the Hölder scale.

Theorem 2 (Approximation Rate of the Daubechies Basis)

Let the underlying trend $f$ belong to the Hölder space $C^\alpha(\mathbb{R})$ with $\alpha \le N$, and let the wavelet $\psi$ possess $N$ vanishing moments. Then the $J$-th level projection $P_{V_J}$ satisfies $$\|f - P_{V_J} f\|_{L^2} \le C_\psi\, 2^{-J\alpha} \|f\|_{C^\alpha}.$$ The estimate follows by expanding $f - P_{V_J}f$ in the detail spaces, applying Parseval's identity, and controlling a single coefficient through the vanishing-moment property: Taylor expansion on the support $I_{j,k}$ of $\psi_{j,k}$ annihilates the polynomial part, leaving $|d_{j,k}| \le C_1 2^{-j(\alpha + 1/2)}$. Summing the $\asymp 2^j$ non-zero coefficients at scale $j$ gives $\sum_k |d_{j,k}|^2 \asymp C_1^2 2^{-2j\alpha}$, and the geometric series over $j \ge J$ contributes the factor $(1 - 2^{-2\alpha})^{-1}$.

The decomposition depth is not a tuning choice but a constrained minimization. Writing $H(c_J)$ for the Shannon entropy of the normalized coefficients, the admissible set is delimited by the growth of the equivalent filter support, $L_j = 1 + (L-1)(2^j - 1)$, and the requirement $L_J \le N$.

Lemma 1 (Decomposition Level Selection)

For a discrete signal $x \in \mathbb{R}^N$ processed by a wavelet filter of length $L$, the decomposition level is selected by $$J^\ast = \arg\min_J \{ H(c_J) + \lambda J \}, \qquad \text{subject to } J < \log_2\!\left(\frac{N}{L-1} + 1\right).$$ Since $0 \le H(c_J) \le \log N$ on the compact simplex and the admissible set $\mathcal{D} = \{1,\dots,J_{\max}\}$ is finite and non-empty, a global minimizer exists. The constraint is not cosmetic: over-decomposition inflates boundary artifacts and spectral leakage, while under-decomposition fails to sparsify the signal.

The volatility channel rests on a spectral separation property. The Hilbert-Huang transform is widely used for instantaneous frequency analysis, but its empirical mode decomposition offers no analytic control over leakage between modes. The Bedrosian condition supplies exactly that control, and it is verified here rather than assumed.

Theorem 3 (Energy Conservation and the Bedrosian Identity)

Let $x \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ be real-valued and let $z = x + i\mathscr{H}x = A e^{i\phi}$ be the associated analytic signal. Then $\|A\|_{L^2}^2 = 2\|x\|_{L^2}^2$. The Hilbert transform is the Fourier multiplier $m(\omega) = -i\,\mathrm{sgn}(\omega)$, whose modulus is unity for $\omega \neq 0$, so $\mathscr{H}$ acts as a linear isometry on $L^2$ and the conservation law follows from Plancherel. If moreover $x(t) = a(t)\cos\phi(t)$ with $\operatorname{supp}(\hat{a}) \subseteq [-B,B]$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\widehat{\cos\phi}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}\setminus[-B,B]$, the disjointness of the supports lets the signum factor pass through the convolution unchanged, yielding $\mathscr{H}\{a(t)\cos\phi(t)\} = a(t)\sin\phi(t)$ and hence the exact envelope $A(t) = |a(t)|$.

Hölder $\alpha$: Level $J$: Bandwidth $B$:
Interactive figure — drag to pan the time axis, scroll to zoom, click a scale band, a decomposition level or a budget term to read its value. The bandwidth control moves the pair $(\hat{a}, \widehat{\cos\phi})$ between disjoint and overlapping spectral supports, so the Bedrosian residual $\|r_{\text{Bedrosian}}\|_{L^2}$ can be watched inflating the envelope error as the separation hypothesis is relaxed.

These two channels combine into a single reliability statement. The estimate is deterministic rather than distributional: it does not assert that the error is small with high probability, but bounds it by three named quantities, each traceable to one structural assumption.

Proposition 4 (Error Bound Decomposition)

Assume the input consists of a regularity-dominated trend and a volatility component. The total prediction error admits the bound $$\mathcal{E}_{\text{total}} \;\le\; \underbrace{C_1 2^{-J\alpha}}_{\text{wavelet approximation}} \;+\; \underbrace{C_2 \|r_{\text{Bedrosian}}\|_{L^2}}_{\text{spectral leakage}} \;+\; \underbrace{C_3 \frac{\sigma_\epsilon^2}{1 - \|\Phi\|_1}}_{\text{AR stability}},$$ where $r_{\text{Bedrosian}}$ measures the violation of the spectral separation condition and $\|\Phi\|_1$ is the $\ell^1$ norm of the autoregressive coefficients, constrained by $\sum_{i=1}^{p} |\phi_i| < 1$ so that the characteristic roots lie inside the unit circle. Each term is attached to one hypothesis, so a degradation in accuracy can be assigned to a named structural cause.

Empirical Behaviour and the Ablation Hierarchy

On the ETTh1 electricity transformer benchmark the architecture attains RMSE $0.1513$ at horizon $h=24$ and $0.3613$ at $h=96$, on par with the PatchTST baseline ($0.3778$ at $h=96$) and ahead of Informer, LSTM and ARIMA across the horizons $h \in \{24,48,96,192\}$, while retaining $O(N)$ computational complexity against the $O(L^2)$ or $O(L\log L)$ scaling of attention-based models. A detailed ablation reproduces the hierarchy predicted by Proposition 4: removing the autoregressive modelling of the scaling coefficients degrades RMSE by $+33.29\%$, disabling the discrete wavelet decomposition by $+20.43\%$, and omitting the Hilbert channel by $+12.54\%$. The ordering matches the energetic weight of the corresponding term in the bound, which is the behaviour one would want from an error decomposition that is meant to be read rather than merely reported. Cross-domain runs on Beijing PM2.5 and Jena Climate — one highly non-stationary, one strongly seasonal — retain competitive accuracy without dataset-specific reparameterization.

The scope of the guarantees should be stated plainly. What is established are error bounds, not exact recovery; the spectral separation condition is rarely satisfied in real-world series, and when the spectra of the trend and volatility components overlap, the residual $\|r_{\text{Bedrosian}}\|_{L^2}$ inflates the approximation error in a manner the bound records but does not remove. Relaxing that constraint through adaptive basis pursuit, and extending the scalar construction to high-dimensional vector-valued series through Clifford analysis, are the directions this leaves open. The complete proofs, the architecture specification and the experimental configuration are published open-access in Scientific Reports: DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-54363-w

On the Quantitative Weight Dependences of Vector-Valued Multilinear Fractional Operators

The multilinear fractional integral operator $\mathcal{I}_\alpha$, introduced by Kenig and Stein, maps $m$-tuples of locally integrable functions into a target Lebesgue space governed by the multilinear Sobolev homogeneity relation $\frac{1}{p} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{1}{p_i} - \frac{\alpha}{n}$. Within the one-weight Muckenhoupt paradigm, the class $A_{\vec{P},p}$ of Moen supplies the weight condition adapted to this off-diagonal scaling. A structural gap has nevertheless persisted: the multi-indexed, off-diagonal vector-valued norm inequalities for $\mathcal{I}_\alpha$ had remained conceptually unquantified, since the available formulations relied on qualitative limiting techniques that cede control over the growth rate of the operator norm in the weight characteristic. In this work, published in Journal of Inequalities and Applications (2026), we close this gap by tracking that growth explicitly.

The mechanism proceeds in two separated stages. We first discretize the continuous multi-indexed potential kernel onto dyadic annuli, which circumscribes $\mathcal{I}_\alpha$ by localized dyadic averages over a sparse family. This reduction is deterministic: every geometric constant generated by the passage from the continuum to the dyadic grid is carried forward in closed form.

Theorem 5 (Pointwise Sparse Domination for Multilinear Fractional Integrals)

Let $0 < \alpha < mn$ and let $\mathcal{I}_\alpha$ act on $\vec{f} = (f_1,\dots,f_m)$. For every vector of functions with bounded support there exists a sparse family $\mathcal{S}$ such that, for almost every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $$|\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\vec{f})(x)| \le C_{n,m,\alpha} \sum_{Q \in \mathcal{S}} |Q|^{\frac{\alpha}{n}} \Big( \prod_{i=1}^{m} \langle |f_i| \rangle_{Q,1} \Big) \chi_Q(x),$$ where the constant is resolved explicitly as $C_{n,m,\alpha} = \big(2^{mn-\alpha} 6^{mn}\big)\big(2^{m} C_{\text{weak}}^{m} 6^{mn}\big)\big(1-2^{-\alpha}\big)^{-1} 6^{mn}$, and the resulting family is $\eta$-sparse with $\eta = 2^{-(n+1)} 36^{-n}$. The dependence on the fractional exponent $\alpha$ is thereby tracked rather than absorbed.

The second stage lifts this scalar localization to multi-indexed sequence spaces. A direct analysis of vector-valued sparse operators under sequence dualization meets topological obstructions — non-convexity in the lower sequence regimes and instability at the $L^1$ endpoint. We bypass these by a decoupling scheme: an explicit scalar weighted bound for the sparse operator within the LMS-range $\max_i p_i' \le p(1-\alpha/n)$, followed by the off-diagonal extrapolation mechanism of Cao, Olivo and Yabuta, specialized to the exact multilinear Sobolev parameters. The weight-characteristic function transfers to the $\ell^r/\ell^{r_i}$ setting without modification.

Theorem 9 (Quantitative Vector-Valued Multilinear Inequalities)

Fix $0 < \alpha < mn$ and exponents $1 < p_1,\dots,p_m < \infty$ satisfying the multilinear Sobolev homogeneity relation with $p \ge 1$. Impose the structural condition $\max_i p_i' \le p(1-\alpha/n)$, let $\vec{w} \in A_{\vec{P},p}$, and fix an inner aggregation tuple $\vec{r} \in \mathcal{R}_\alpha$. Then $$\Big\| \Big( \sum_k |\mathcal{I}_\alpha(f_{1,k},\dots,f_{m,k})|^r \Big)^{1/r} \Big\|_{L^p_{\nu_{\vec{w}}}} \le C\, [\vec{w}]_{A_{\vec{P},p}}^{\tilde{\kappa}} \prod_{i=1}^{m} \Big\| \Big( \sum_k |f_{i,k}|^{r_i} \Big)^{1/r_i} \Big\|_{L^{p_i}_{w_i}},$$ with explicit exponent $\tilde{\kappa} = p\left(1 - \frac{\alpha}{n}\right)$, where $\frac{1}{r} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{1}{r_i}$ and $C = C_{n,m,\vec{P},\alpha,\vec{r}}$ is deterministic in $\vec{w}$.

Fractional order $\alpha/n$:
Interactive figure — drag to pan the dyadic grid, scroll to zoom the stopping-time recursion, click a cube to inspect its localized average. The sparse selection threshold $a = 2^{m} C_{\text{weak}}^{m} 6^{mn}$ guarantees $|E_P| \ge \frac{1}{2}|P|$; the exponent panel traces $\tilde{\kappa} = p(1-\alpha/n)$ across the admissible range delimited by the structural condition.
Key Takeaway: Quantitative rather than Qualitative

The entire weight-dependence of the estimate is concentrated in the single factor $[\vec{w}]_{A_{\vec{P},p}}^{\tilde{\kappa}}$; the residual constant is deterministic in $\vec{w}$. The estimate therefore exhibits in closed form the analytic rate at which the operator norm degrades as the weight characteristic grows, in contrast to an exponent accessible only as the unquantified output of an abstract limiting procedure. A single inequality governs the scalar and vector-valued regimes at once: restricting the sequence to one non-zero tuple collapses the inner aggregations and returns the scalar weighted bound, so the vector-valued extension is obtained at no cost in the weight exponent. Within the range delimited by the structural condition and the fractional positivity condition, $\tilde{\kappa}$ is on par with the scalar benchmark of Lacey, Moen, Pérez and Torres after conversion between the un-renormalized and renormalized weight conventions.

The borderline regime $p \to 1$ and weak-type endpoint estimates lie outside the present range and are not addressed by this method. The analysis is moreover carried out for the standard multilinear fractional kernel; an extension to rough fractional kernels would proceed by replacing the discretization step with a sparse domination adapted to the weaker kernel hypotheses, after which the extrapolation mechanism transfers without modification. The complete proofs and explicit constant derivations are published open-access in Journal of Inequalities and Applications: DOI: 10.1186/s13660-026-03511-x

Explicit Approximation Rates for Shallow Neural Networks on Additive Besov Classes: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality

In mathematical machine learning and constructive approximation theory, a central challenge is overcoming the curse of dimensionality. When approximating functions on bounded Lipschitz domains $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ using single-hidden-layer neural networks, classical Jackson estimates on the Besov scale $B^s_{p,q}(\Omega)$ yield error decay rates of order $N^{-s/d}$ with network width $N$. As ambient dimension $d$ grows, this convergence rate rapidly degrades. In our recent work published in Mathematics (2026, 14(14), 2491), we establish explicit, non-asymptotic approximation error bounds for localized shallow networks, prove a univariate inverse Bernstein converse on nonlinear free-knot Besov spaces, and demonstrate that on coordinate-subset additive Besov classes $\mathcal{S}^s_{d_0}(\Omega)$, the approximation rate is governed solely by the effective dimension $d_0$, with the ambient dimension $d$ entering only through the explicit prefactor constant.

Theorem 5 (Direct Jackson-Type Estimate for Localized Shallow Networks)

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Let $\sigma$ satisfy standing regularity hypotheses (A1)–(A3) and admit an exact spline generator $\Lambda \in \mathcal{N}_{\nu_0}(\sigma; 1)$ of order $W \ge r_\sigma + 1$ reproducing polynomials of degree $\le r_\sigma$. For $1 \le p \le \infty$, $0 < q \le \infty$, and $0 < s < s_\sigma = r_\sigma + 1$: $$E_N^\flat(f)_{L_p(\Omega)} \le C_J N^{-s/d} |f|_{B^s_{p,q}(\Omega)}, \quad \forall N \ge N_0$$ where $C_J = C_J(\sigma, s, p, q, d, \Omega) > 0$ is explicitly tracked through the activation parameters $(K_\sigma, m_\sigma, r_\sigma, \nu_0, W)$ and the Lipschitz extension constant $C_W(\Omega)$ via the homogeneous $K$-functional $K(f, t^r; L_p, \dot{W}^r_p) \asymp \omega_r(f, t)_{L_p}$.

In one dimension ($d=1$), we establish the corresponding converse theorem on the nonlinear diagonal Besov scale, characterizing the approximation space of localized neural networks:

Corollary 1 (Univariate Converse / Inverse Bernstein Estimate on $B^\alpha_{\tau,\tau}$)

Let $d=1, \Omega=(0,1)$ and $\sigma = \text{ReLU}^k$ ($s_\sigma = k+1$). If $f \in L_p(\Omega)$ ($1 \le p < \infty$) satisfies the dyadic $\ell_\tau$-summability condition for $0 < \alpha < s_\sigma$ and $\frac{1}{\tau} = \alpha + \frac{1}{p}$: $$|f|_{\mathcal{A}} := \left[ \sum_{j \ge 0} \left( 2^{j\alpha} E_{2^j}^\flat(f)_{L_p(\Omega)} \right)^\tau \right]^{1/\tau} \le A < \infty$$ then $f \in B^\alpha_{\tau,\tau}(\Omega)$ on the nonlinear free-knot Besov scale, and $\|f\|_{B^\alpha_{\tau,\tau}(\Omega)} \le C' (\|f\|_{L_p(\Omega)} + A)$ with explicit $C' = C'(k, \alpha, p)$.

The principal breakthrough of this work is the effective-dimension refinement. On a bounded product domain $\Omega = \prod_{i=1}^d \Omega_i$, functions in the coordinate-subset additive Besov class $\mathcal{S}^s_{d_0}(\Omega) = \{f(x) = \sum_{|T|=d_0} g_T(x_T) : g_T \in B^s_{p,q}(\Omega_T)\}$ carry $d_0$-variate coordinate interactions ($1 \le d_0 \le d$):

Theorem 6 (Effective-Dimension Refinement on Additive Besov Classes)

For every $f \in \mathcal{S}^s_{d_0}(\Omega)$ and $N \ge N_0''$: $$E_N^\flat(f)_{L_p(\Omega)} \le C'' N^{-s/d_0} |f|_{\mathcal{S}^s_{d_0}(\Omega)}$$ The decay exponent $-s/d_0$ depends strictly on the effective dimension $d_0$. The ambient dimension $d$ enters only through the explicit prefactor constant $C'' = \Lambda C_1 (2\kappa)^{s/d_0} \binom{d}{d_0}^{s/d_0}$, where $\kappa = \frac{\nu' + d\nu''}{\nu' + d_0\nu''}$ is the localized coordinate embedding factor and $\Lambda$ is the geometric fiber measure bound.

Key Takeaway & Interpretability in Applied Learning

By distributing the width budget across coordinate-subset faces via deterministic least-squares projections, we achieve dimensional rate decoupling without iterative optimization variance. On educational tabular datasets (UCI Student Performance), held-out $L_2$ diagnostics confirm that target prediction is governed by effective dimension $d_0 = 1$, validating that feature-parsimonious, explainable additive architectures prevent overfitting to spurious high-order coordinate noise.

The complete proofs, explicit constant derivations, and empirical validation scripts are published open-access in Mathematics: DOI: 10.3390/math14142491

Constructive approximation theory often establishes asymptotic convergence orders without displaying explicit constants. Theorem 1 (Direct Jackson Estimate) & Theorem 2 (Inverse Bernstein Estimate)

When $w$ is locally comparable to Lebesgue measure, the effective convergence rate is exactly: $$\text{Effective Decay Rate} = \min\left(s, \frac{1}{p}\right)$$

On the Geometric Phase-Space Obstructions in Wavelet Frames: Understanding the Anisotropic Balian-Low Theorem

In time-frequency analysis and multiscale representation theory, a fundamental tension exists between the smoothness of a generator window and its phase-space localization. In classical Gabor analysis (Weyl-Heisenberg systems), this limitation is famously codified by the Balian-Low Theorem (BLT).

Classical Balian-Low Theorem (Gabor Case)

Let $g \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and consider the Gabor system $\mathcal{G}(g, \alpha, \beta) = \{e^{2\pi i m \beta x} g(x - n \alpha)\}_{m,n \in \mathbb{Z}}$. If $\alpha \beta = 1$ and $\mathcal{G}(g, \alpha, \beta)$ forms a Riesz basis for $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, then: $$\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |x g(x)|^2 dx\right) \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |\xi \hat{g}(\xi)|^2 d\xi\right) = +\infty$$

That is, a Riesz basis of Gabor atoms cannot have simultaneous second-order localization in both position and frequency. When moving from the lattice translations of Gabor systems to the affine scaling groups of Wavelet bi-frames, how does this obstruction transform, particularly in higher dimensions under anisotropic dilation matrices?

Interactive Figure: Phase-space Heisenberg uncertainty area $\Delta x \cdot \Delta \xi \ge 1/2$. The area of the ellipse is invariant under symplectic transforms, but geometric anisotropy induces directional obstruction.
Key Research Insight

For anisotropic wavelet frames generated by expansive matrices $A \in \text{GL}(d, \mathbb{R})$, the geometric obstruction is characterized by the spectral distribution of the generator matrix and the geometry of the cone singularities in the frequency domain. This connects directly with the weighted Besov decay conditions and sharp Jackson-type estimates.

Bedrosian Identity Analytic Signal Instantaneous Frequency AM-FM Signals October 2026 15 min read

From Bedrosian to AM-FM Decomposition: What the Analytic Signal Recovers, and What It Cannot

A real signal written as $x(t) = a(t)\cos\theta(t)$ with $a \ge 0$ is said to carry the amplitude $a$ and the instantaneous frequency $\theta'/2\pi$. The pair $(a, \theta)$ is not determined by $x$ alone, so a convention must select one. Gabor's convention is the analytic signal $z = x + i\,\mathscr H x$, which retains only the positive frequencies of $x$, doubled: $\hat z(\xi) = 2\hat x(\xi)\mathbf 1_{\{\xi > 0\}}$. One then reads $a_z = |z|$ and $\theta_z = \arg z$. The question of this note is when $(a_z, \theta_z)$ is the pair one had in mind, which is the same as asking when $\mathscr H[a\cos\theta] = a\sin\theta$. For a pure carrier $\theta = \omega_0 t$ the answer is Bedrosian's theorem; for a frequency-modulated carrier the answer is an explicit series, and the figure below evaluates it next to the measured error.

Theorem 1 (Bedrosian, 1963)

Let $f, g \in L^2(\mathbb R)$ with $\operatorname{supp}\hat f \subset [-B, B]$ and $\operatorname{supp}\hat g \subset \{|\xi| \ge B\}$. Then $\mathscr H(fg) = f\,\mathscr H g$. In particular, if $a$ has spectrum in $[-B, B]$ and $\omega_0 > 2\pi B$, then $\mathscr H[a(t)\cos\omega_0 t] = a(t)\sin\omega_0 t$ and the analytic signal of $a\cos\omega_0 t$ is exactly $a\,e^{i\omega_0 t}$, so that $|z| = a$ and the instantaneous frequency equals $\omega_0/2\pi$.

Theorem 2 (Mean-square error of the analytic signal of an FM carrier)

Let $x(t) = \cos(\omega_0 t + \beta\sin\omega_m t)$, with $\omega_0, \omega_m > 0$ and a common period, and let $z_{\rm true} = e^{i(\omega_0 t + \beta \sin\omega_m t)}$. Then, averaged over one common period, $$\overline{\,|z - z_{\rm true}|^2\,} \;=\; 2\sum_{k:\ \omega_0 + k\omega_m < 0} J_k(\beta)^2 \;=\; 2\sum_{|k| > \omega_0/\omega_m} J_k(\beta)^2 .$$ Proof. The Jacobi-Anger expansion gives $z_{\rm true} = \sum_k J_k(\beta)\,e^{i\omega_k t}$ with $\omega_k = \omega_0 + k\omega_m$ and real coefficients, and $x = \mathrm{Re}\,z_{\rm true}$. The analytic signal keeps each term with $\omega_k > 0$ unchanged, and replaces each term with $\omega_k < 0$ by its mirror image $J_k e^{-i\omega_k t}$; a term with $\omega_k = 0$ is unchanged. The difference is therefore $-2i\sum_{\omega_k < 0} J_k \sin(\omega_k t)$, and the sinusoids have distinct frequencies $|\omega_k|$, so their mean squares add, each equal to $2J_k^2$. $\square$

Signal:
Carrier $f_c$:Modulation $f_m$:Index $\beta$:
Interactive figure. All tones are integer frequencies on a period of length 1 with 1024 samples, so the FFT-based analytic signal is exact on the grid. Time domain: for AM, $x = (1 + 0.8\cos 2\pi f_m t)\cos 2\pi f_c t$; the recovered envelope $|z|$ coincides with $a$ as long as $f_m < f_c$ and departs from it once $f_m > f_c$ (button 24 with carrier 16). For FM the instantaneous frequency from the analytic signal is drawn against $f_c + \beta f_m\cos 2\pi f_m t$. Spectrum: the gold lines at negative frequency are the components discarded by the analytic signal. Error against $\beta$: the dots are the measured mean-square errors for $\beta = 0, 0.25, \dots, 14$; the curve is the series of Theorem 2, evaluated with Bessel functions computed by quadrature. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, hover to read values.

The tail of the series explains an engineering rule of thumb. For $|k| > \beta$ the Bessel coefficients $J_k(\beta)$ decay faster than any geometric rate, because $J_k(\beta) \sim (\beta/2)^k/k!$, so the sum in Theorem 2 is negligible as soon as the first negative-frequency index $\lfloor \omega_0/\omega_m\rfloor + 1$ exceeds $\beta$ by a few multiples of $\beta^{1/3}$. In words: the carrier frequency must exceed the peak frequency deviation $\beta f_m$ by a modest margin, which is the one-sided counterpart of Carson's bandwidth rule. In the error panel this appears as a plateau at rounding level followed by a rapid rise at the value of $\beta$ where $J_{k_0}(\beta)$ leaves its exponentially small range. For amplitude modulation the same computation has a single negative component with coefficient $m/2$ when $f_m > f_c$, giving a mean-square error exactly $m^2/2$, in agreement with the residual formula of the earlier Bedrosian note.

A decomposition needs a declared convention

The analytic signal is a principled convention, not a fact about the signal: it returns the pair $(a, \theta)$ intended by the modeller exactly when the spectral separation of Theorem 1 holds, and otherwise it returns a different, equally well-defined pair, whose distance from the intended one is the quantity computed in Theorem 2. Methods that do not rely on a global Fourier projection, such as empirical mode decomposition, replace the spectral hypothesis by a local one on extrema, and they carry their own conventions. Reporting an instantaneous frequency therefore calls for naming the convention used and, where possible, the size of the discrepancy it can induce.

Three limitations should be kept in view. The identity in Theorem 2 is an exact statement about periodic signals sampled on the grid; for a finite record with edges, window effects add errors that it does not describe. The phase derivative used to read the instantaneous frequency amplifies noise, so even a perfect analytic signal gives a noisy frequency estimate on measured data. Finally, nothing here addresses multicomponent signals, for which the analytic signal of a sum is the sum of analytic signals but the modulus and phase of a sum are not the moduli and phases of the parts.
